**Luigi Tenco** (21 March 1938 – 27 January 1967) was an Italian singer-songwriter. He died on the night of 27 January 1967 after a performance at the [Sanremo Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Music_Festival_1967 "Sanremo Music Festival 1967"). His death was ruled to be the result of suicide, but even decades later, a plethora of evidence in favor of murder was cause to reopen the investigation twice.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Tenco was born in [Cassine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassine,_Piedmont "Cassine, Piedmont") ([province of Alessandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Alessandria "Province of Alessandria")) in 1938, the son of Teresa Zoccola. He never knew his father. Teresa Zoccola was married to Giuseppe Tenco, and they had a son, Valentino, but the couple eventually separated, and Teresa moved to Cassine. It has been rumoured that Luigi Tenco was the product of an extramarital relationship between his mother and an unidentified man of the Micca family, for whom she worked at the time: potentially the sixteen-year-old son or his father. When Zoccola discovered the pregnancy, she returned to Cassine. The boy was given the name of her husband, Tenco, who died in a work accident while she was several months pregnant.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)

Tenco spent his childhood in Cassine and [Ricaldone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricaldone "Ricaldone") until 1948, when he moved to [Liguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liguria "Liguria"), first to [Nervi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nervi "Nervi") and then to [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), where his mother had a wine shop called _Enos_ in the quarter of La Foce. He developed an early interest in music, teaching himself to play guitar, clarinet and saxophone. During high school, Tenco founded the [Jelly Roll Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton "Jelly Roll Morton") Boys Jazz band, in which Tenco played the clarinet and [Bruno Lauzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_Lauzi "Bruno Lauzi"), another singer later to become famous, played [banjo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banjo "Banjo"). [Gino Paoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Paoli "Gino Paoli"), who would become one of Italy's most famous singers and songwriters, also played with Tenco in the band he was later involved in, I Diavoli del Rock (The Rock Devils).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)

Tenco made his debut in the world of Italian professional music with the band I Cavalieri (The Knights), which included [Giampiero Reverberi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gian_Piero_Reverberi "Gian Piero Reverberi") and [Enzo Jannacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Jannacci "Enzo Jannacci") amongst others. During this period, he used the pseudonym Gigi Mai. In 1961, Tenco released his first single under his real name, entitled _Quando_ ("When").

He started university studying [electronic engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_engineering "Electronic engineering"), trying to comply with the wishes of his mother and brother. He twice failed the Analytic and Projective Geometry exam (a course he took with professor [Eugenio Giuseppe Togliatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenio_Giuseppe_Togliatti "Eugenio Giuseppe Togliatti"), the elder brother of Communist party leader [Palmiro Togliatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmiro_Togliatti "Palmiro Togliatti")). Later, he was enrolled in [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science"), where he gave only two exams.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)

Tenco was interested in cinema and videomaking. In 1962, he began a short-lived cinematic experience, with [Luciano Salce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Salce "Luciano Salce")'s movie _[La Cuccagna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Girl...\_and\_a\_Million "A Girl... and a Million")_. He also collaborated on the soundtrack of the film, and introduced his friend [Fabrizio De André](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9 "Fabrizio De André") (unknown at the time) through the song _La ballata dell'eroe_ (_Ballad for a hero_).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-2) Director [Luigi Comencini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Comencini "Luigi Comencini") considered Tenco for the role of Bube in his film _[La ragazza di Bube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_ragazza\_di\_Bube\_(film) "La ragazza di Bube (film)")_, based on [Carlo Cassola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Cassola "Carlo Cassola")'s novel. He ultimately chose [George Chakiris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Chakiris "George Chakiris"), the _[West Side Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West\_Side\_Story "West Side Story")_ star, instead. During this period, Tenco formed a strong friendship with the Genoese [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchism "Anarchism") poet Riccardo Mannerini. In 1963, however, his friendship with Gino Paoli broke up, due to a troubled relationship with the actress [Stefania Sandrelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefania_Sandrelli "Stefania Sandrelli").

Tenco's first [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramophone_record "Gramophone record"), _Ballate e Canzoni_, was released in 1962. One of the songs, "Cara maestra" ("Dear Teacher"), was censored by the then-thriving Italian media censorship. For this song, he was banned from [Rai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAI "RAI") for two years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTECampanellaPalmieri2017-3)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDe_AngelisDeregibus2013-4) The censors struck again in the following year, against his songs "Io sì" ("I Would"), considered too sexually explicit, and "Una brava ragazza" ("A Good Girl"), where Tenco express his admiration for a '60s "bad girl". In September 1964, he released "[Ho capito che ti amo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_capito_che_ti_amo "Ho capito che ti amo")", a song written by him with musical arrangement by [Ezio Leoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezio_Leoni "Ezio Leoni"). It was released on the Italian record label [Jolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jolly_(record_company) "Jolly (record company)") as Side A of a 45 rpm, side B being "Io lo so già".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-5) In [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), "Ho capito che ti amo" was the soundtrack of the popular soap opera _[El amor tiene cara de mujer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_amor\_tiene\_cara\_de\_mujer\_(Argentine\_TV\_series) "El amor tiene cara de mujer (Argentine TV series)")_.

In 1966, enduring a period of compulsory military service, he released "Un giorno dopo l'altro" (_One Day after Another_) for [RCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation "RCA Corporation"). The military service did not stop him from travelling to Argentina together with [Gianfranco Reverberi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gian_Franco_Reverberi "Gian Franco Reverberi") to meet the fans of _El amor tiene cara de mujer_. How he managed to arrive in Argentina while his passport was still in possession of the Italian Army is unknown. Moreover, under the military service, one was not allowed to leave Italy, and the punishment was detention, which he did not experience according to his service record book.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

In [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") during the same year, he met and befriended the Italian-French singer [Dalida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalida "Dalida"). It was widely assumed that they became lovers; however, Tenco had a fiancée, Valeria, to whom, a decade after his death, many letters were discovered. Tenco's mother also confirmed that he treated Dalida only as a good friend.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-7) Lino Patruno, a close friend of Tenco, described his relationship with Dalida as a 'marketing trick'.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-corriere2021-8)

## 1967 Sanremo Festival and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1967 Sanremo Festival and death")]

In January 1967, Tenco took part in the [Sanremo Music Festival 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Music_Festival_1967 "Sanremo Music Festival 1967"). It was rumoured that he participated against his will. On 26 January he performed the song "[Ciao amore, ciao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciao_amore,_ciao "Ciao amore, ciao")" ("Bye Bye, My Love") with [Dalida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalida "Dalida"). The video of the performance is lost; however, the audio track, recorded from the radio, survives.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-9) That evening, Tenco sang badly and off time, presumably because he had taken [barbiturates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbiturate "Barbiturate") with alcohol shortly before the performance to cope with anxiety.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-10) Later that evening he was seen at the Nostromo restaurant together with Dalida, other friends and colleagues. He left early, leaving the group behind.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

At approximately 2 in the morning of 27 January, Tenco was found dead in his room, No. 219, at the Hotel Savoy by Dalida.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-12) Tenco died from a single gunshot wound to the head. His death was ultimately ruled a suicide.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-:1-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-nytimes-14) However, due to multiple violations in the investigation, the case was reopened twice, still with a verdict of a suicide.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Tenco was apparently upset after learning that his song had been eliminated from the final competition.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-nytimes-14) Several people close to Tenco witnessed that he was more upset with the corruption and bribery at the festival and planned to hold a press conference to unveil it all.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-corriere2021-8)

Tenco was buried in Ricaldone in a small ceremony, while the festival officials kept the show going and tried to evade a scandal. Almost no colleagues were present at the funeral.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-15)

### The inquiry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The inquiry")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Tomba_Luigi_Tenco.jpg/250px-Tomba_Luigi_Tenco.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tomba_Luigi_Tenco.jpg)

Grave of Luigi Tenco

Initially ruled as a suicide, Tenco's case was reopened in 2005–2009 and then again in 2013–2015.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-17)

In 2004, on TV program _[Domenica in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenica\_in "Domenica in")_, commissario Arrigo Molinari, the detective who led the case, when asked by host [Paolo Bonolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Bonolis "Paolo Bonolis"), stated that he was sure that Tenco did not commit suicide and defined his death as "a collective murder".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-18) He also justified his own faults concerning the Tenco inquiry by declaring that he had been prevented from investigating properly. In 1967, upon learning of Tenco's death from Dalida and still in his own home, Molinari phoned ANSA and declared that the singer had killed himself. All this took place before he had arrived at the Savoy and before the forensic team could intervene. Shortly after the quoted 2004 interview, Molinari was stabbed to death in his own hotel in [Andora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andora "Andora").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

In 1967, no [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") was performed on the singer's corpse, and no paraffin test or calligraphic analysis on the [suicide note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_note "Suicide note") with which he explained his final gesture were done.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-19) Some police photographs from the scene, unedited and publicly shown only in 1994, showed that Tenco's body and face was bruised. On the back side of his head a trauma was evident, which forensics didn't confirm to be related to post-mortem falling. Additionally, the concierge of the Savoy, when asked if he had seen Tenco return that night, stated that the keys were not on the reception desk and not that he had seen Tenco return. Traces of sand were spotted on Tenco's hair, clothes and in his car, though journalists confirmed that the car was washed before going to Nostromo.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Dalida testified that on the night of 26 January, while still at the Nostromo, she received a phone call from the Hotel Londra in Sanremo. She told diners she had been notified that Tenco was at the Savoy and was feeling unwell. Dalida did not rush to the Savoy, which was about five minutes away, instead stopping to buy cigarettes and then picking up her ex-husband, Lucien Morisse. They arrived at the Savoy after 40 minutes, where she discovered Tenco's lifeless body.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Notably, the alleged farewell note does not appear in the police report, as it was not found in room 219 on the night of Tenco's death. In fact, the note came into the hands of the police from a third party. Initially, in Dalida's room, No. 104, she gave it to Tenco's friend Sergio Modugno, who passed it on to Piero Vivarelli, a journalist and another of Tenco's friends, who finally gave it to the police. The note read: "I cared for the Italian public and I dedicated in vain five years of my life to them. I'm doing this not because I'm tired of life (I'm not) but as a gesture of dissent against the public who chose 'Io, tu e le rose' for the final night and against the commission that selected 'La rivoluzione'. I hope this will clear somebody's head." Forensics later detected word casts on the note, as if there had been at least one other sheet with different writing superimposed on the one found. The words in the casts are ‘gioco’ (game) and ‘già’ (already). Game, in particular, would seem compatible with Tenco's intention to denounce clandestine betting, as he had announced to his fiancée Valeria in the above-mentioned telephone call. One of the police photos of commissario Molinari showed him standing at the scene with two sheets of paper. Moreover, experts never confirmed the signature on the note to be Tenco's and noted a spelling mistake that a native speaker of Italian who dealt with writing daily would not have made. The family also didn't recognize the handwriting as Tenco's. As supposed by journalists, the alleged suicide note may have been the last page of a document written by Tenco for a different aim.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-20)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

The Italian judicial system later began re-examining Luigi Tenco's suicide. It was pointed out that the bullet hole was on the left temple, while the singer was right-handed. On 15 February 2006, Italian police exhumed Tenco's body for further investigation.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-exhumation-21) The next day, results from the new [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") and [ballistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistics "Ballistics") analysis were reported. According to Italian experts, what had been thought to be the entry hole on Tenco's left temple was actually the exit site. The bullet [trajectory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajectory "Trajectory") was said to be compatible with suicide.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-:1-13)

Nevertheless, criminologists Pasquale Ragone and Nicola Guarneri, in their book _Le ombre del silenzio_ (_The shadows of silence_, 2013), pointed out several incongruences between the shell casing of the bullet found in Tenco's room and the bullet Tenco's [Walther PPK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_PPK "Walther PPK") handgun would fire. Professor of ballistic forensics Martino Farneti proved that they did not match. As there was no proof or official statement declaring that Tenco's Walther PPK was actually present in his room the night he died, and police registers show that the pistol was actually found in his car, Guarneri and Ragone wrote that Tenco may have been killed. The actual weapon may have been a [Beretta 70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beretta_70 "Beretta 70"), as it is possible to put a silencer on this type of handgun (similar to a Walther PPK). In fact, no one heard the sound of gunshots the night Tenco died, not even singer [Lucio Dalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucio_Dalla "Lucio Dalla"), whose room was next to Tenco's, or journalist Sandro Ciotti, whose room was opposite Tenco's.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6) At the time of Tenco's death, a door to the inner garden was located only three meters from room 2019, the same one used by police to transport the body.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

In 1993, journalists Marco Buttazzi and Andrea Pomati rediscovered the file compiled by the police in 1967. In the attached photos, they saw that Tenco's legs (from ankles to feet) were positioned under a wooden cabinet. Suspicious of the anomalous position of the corpse, they investigated further and found out that the photos did not depict the real crime scene. They interviewed the undertaker from the case, who stated that commissario Molinari had ordered the body to be immediately transferred to the morgue and before the arrival of the forensic team; it was then taken back to the Savoy and reassembled to allow the photos to be taken and attached to the above-mentioned file.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Music producer and friend [Paolo Dossena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Dossena "Paolo Dossena") stated that he drove Tenco's car from Rome, where the songwriter lived, to Sanremo. On the way, while passing through a roadblock on the [Aurelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Aurelia "Via Aurelia"), he discovered that Tenco had his Walther PPK in the dashboard of his car. He later confronted the songwriter, who confessed that he had a gun because someone in the past few weeks had tried to force him off a steep road near [Santa Margherita Ligure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Margherita_Ligure "Santa Margherita Ligure") while he was driving.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolteni2015-23)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

In the early '90s, Tenco's older brother Valentino met a woman, Valeria, who had in her possession several letters written by Tenco himself that stated that they had been engaged, their relationship starting in 1964 and lasting until his death. In one of these letters, Tenco writes that his relationship with Dalida was nothing but a clumsy attempt to forget Valeria, who, months before, had left him. He describes Dalida as: "spoiled, neurotic, ignorant, who rejects the idea of being defeated in her profession as in private life". Valentino Tenco identified those letters as written by his brother.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

To date, besides the official conclusion of suicide, journalists have come up with three theories:

*   A robbery gone bad — on 26 January, Tenco won almost 3 million liras at a casino, but the money was never found after his death;
*   A murder of jealousy — Morisse, Dalida's ex-husband, was seen leaving room 219. Morisse was known as an incredibly jealous man who tried to control Dalida and her affairs even after their divorce;
*   A murder to prevent Tenco from causing a scandal by uncovering the bribery and corruption schemes at the Sanremo Festival.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Tributes")]

Shortly after Tenco's death, his friend and songwriter Fabrizio De André wrote the song _Preghiera in gennaio_ (A prayer in January) for him, in which he describes a benevolent God welcoming those who committed suicide into Heaven despite the moral condemnation of the bigots.

In 1974, the [Tenco Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Tenco "Club Tenco") was established, and has been held every year since in Sanremo. Many of the most renowned Italian singer-songwriters from the 1970s explicitly declared Tenco's influence on their work. [Francesco De Gregori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_De_Gregori "Francesco De Gregori")'s album _[Bufalo Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bufalo\_Bill "Bufalo Bill")_ of 1976 contained a song, "Festival", about Tenco's suicide; it points out the hypocrisy with which the music establishment tried to minimize the dramatic event, to let the show go on.

In 1999, the play _Solitudini – Luigi Tenco e [Dalida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalida "Dalida")_, written and directed by Maurizio Valtieri, was performed in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").

French journalist and novelist Philippe Brunel wrote a fiction book, _La nuit de San Remo_ ("The night of Sanremo"), in which he dramatises the arduous search for the truth about Tenco's death.

In 2005, the French television channel [TV5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV5MONDE "TV5MONDE") carried a full-length dramatisation of the love affair between Tenco and Dalida. Tenco was played by [Alessandro Gassman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Gassman "Alessandro Gassman"), and Dalida by [Sabrina Ferilli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabrina_Ferilli "Sabrina Ferilli").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

Musical artist

**Luigi Tenco** (21 March 1938 – 27 January 1967) was an Italian singer-songwriter. He died on the night of 27 January 1967 after a performance at the [Sanremo Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Music_Festival_1967 "Sanremo Music Festival 1967"). His death was ruled to be the result of suicide, but even decades later, a plethora of evidence in favor of murder was cause to reopen the investigation twice.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Tenco was born in [Cassine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassine,_Piedmont "Cassine, Piedmont") ([province of Alessandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Alessandria "Province of Alessandria")) in 1938, the son of Teresa Zoccola. He never knew his father. Teresa Zoccola was married to Giuseppe Tenco, and they had a son, Valentino, but the couple eventually separated, and Teresa moved to Cassine. It has been rumoured that Luigi Tenco was the product of an extramarital relationship between his mother and an unidentified man of the Micca family, for whom she worked at the time: potentially the sixteen-year-old son or his father. When Zoccola discovered the pregnancy, she returned to Cassine. The boy was given the name of her husband, Tenco, who died in a work accident while she was several months pregnant.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)

Tenco spent his childhood in Cassine and [Ricaldone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricaldone "Ricaldone") until 1948, when he moved to [Liguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liguria "Liguria"), first to [Nervi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nervi "Nervi") and then to [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), where his mother had a wine shop called _Enos_ in the quarter of La Foce. He developed an early interest in music, teaching himself to play guitar, clarinet and saxophone. During high school, Tenco founded the [Jelly Roll Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jelly_Roll_Morton "Jelly Roll Morton") Boys Jazz band, in which Tenco played the clarinet and [Bruno Lauzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_Lauzi "Bruno Lauzi"), another singer later to become famous, played [banjo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banjo "Banjo"). [Gino Paoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Paoli "Gino Paoli"), who would become one of Italy's most famous singers and songwriters, also played with Tenco in the band he was later involved in, I Diavoli del Rock (The Rock Devils).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)

Tenco made his debut in the world of Italian professional music with the band I Cavalieri (The Knights), which included [Giampiero Reverberi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gian_Piero_Reverberi "Gian Piero Reverberi") and [Enzo Jannacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Jannacci "Enzo Jannacci") amongst others. During this period, he used the pseudonym Gigi Mai. In 1961, Tenco released his first single under his real name, entitled _Quando_ ("When").

He started university studying [electronic engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_engineering "Electronic engineering"), trying to comply with the wishes of his mother and brother. He twice failed the Analytic and Projective Geometry exam (a course he took with professor [Eugenio Giuseppe Togliatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenio_Giuseppe_Togliatti "Eugenio Giuseppe Togliatti"), the elder brother of Communist party leader [Palmiro Togliatti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmiro_Togliatti "Palmiro Togliatti")). Later, he was enrolled in [political science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_science "Political science"), where he gave only two exams.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)

Tenco was interested in cinema and videomaking. In 1962, he began a short-lived cinematic experience, with [Luciano Salce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Salce "Luciano Salce")'s movie _[La Cuccagna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Girl...\_and\_a\_Million "A Girl... and a Million")_. He also collaborated on the soundtrack of the film, and introduced his friend [Fabrizio De André](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabrizio_De_Andr%C3%A9 "Fabrizio De André") (unknown at the time) through the song _La ballata dell'eroe_ (_Ballad for a hero_).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-2) Director [Luigi Comencini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Comencini "Luigi Comencini") considered Tenco for the role of Bube in his film _[La ragazza di Bube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_ragazza\_di\_Bube\_(film) "La ragazza di Bube (film)")_, based on [Carlo Cassola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlo_Cassola "Carlo Cassola")'s novel. He ultimately chose [George Chakiris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Chakiris "George Chakiris"), the _[West Side Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West\_Side\_Story "West Side Story")_ star, instead. During this period, Tenco formed a strong friendship with the Genoese [anarchist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anarchism "Anarchism") poet Riccardo Mannerini. In 1963, however, his friendship with Gino Paoli broke up, due to a troubled relationship with the actress [Stefania Sandrelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stefania_Sandrelli "Stefania Sandrelli").

Tenco's first [LP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gramophone_record "Gramophone record"), _Ballate e Canzoni_, was released in 1962. One of the songs, "Cara maestra" ("Dear Teacher"), was censored by the then-thriving Italian media censorship. For this song, he was banned from [Rai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAI "RAI") for two years.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTECampanellaPalmieri2017-3)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDe_AngelisDeregibus2013-4) The censors struck again in the following year, against his songs "Io sì" ("I Would"), considered too sexually explicit, and "Una brava ragazza" ("A Good Girl"), where Tenco express his admiration for a '60s "bad girl". In September 1964, he released "[Ho capito che ti amo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ho_capito_che_ti_amo "Ho capito che ti amo")", a song written by him with musical arrangement by [Ezio Leoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezio_Leoni "Ezio Leoni"). It was released on the Italian record label [Jolly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jolly_(record_company) "Jolly (record company)") as Side A of a 45 rpm, side B being "Io lo so già".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-5) In [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), "Ho capito che ti amo" was the soundtrack of the popular soap opera _[El amor tiene cara de mujer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El\_amor\_tiene\_cara\_de\_mujer\_(Argentine\_TV\_series) "El amor tiene cara de mujer (Argentine TV series)")_.

In 1966, enduring a period of compulsory military service, he released "Un giorno dopo l'altro" (_One Day after Another_) for [RCA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Corporation "RCA Corporation"). The military service did not stop him from travelling to Argentina together with [Gianfranco Reverberi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gian_Franco_Reverberi "Gian Franco Reverberi") to meet the fans of _El amor tiene cara de mujer_. How he managed to arrive in Argentina while his passport was still in possession of the Italian Army is unknown. Moreover, under the military service, one was not allowed to leave Italy, and the punishment was detention, which he did not experience according to his service record book.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

In [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") during the same year, he met and befriended the Italian-French singer [Dalida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalida "Dalida"). It was widely assumed that they became lovers; however, Tenco had a fiancée, Valeria, to whom, a decade after his death, many letters were discovered. Tenco's mother also confirmed that he treated Dalida only as a good friend.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-7) Lino Patruno, a close friend of Tenco, described his relationship with Dalida as a 'marketing trick'.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-corriere2021-8)

## 1967 Sanremo Festival and death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1967 Sanremo Festival and death")]

In January 1967, Tenco took part in the [Sanremo Music Festival 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanremo_Music_Festival_1967 "Sanremo Music Festival 1967"). It was rumoured that he participated against his will. On 26 January he performed the song "[Ciao amore, ciao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ciao_amore,_ciao "Ciao amore, ciao")" ("Bye Bye, My Love") with [Dalida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalida "Dalida"). The video of the performance is lost; however, the audio track, recorded from the radio, survives.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-9) That evening, Tenco sang badly and off time, presumably because he had taken [barbiturates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbiturate "Barbiturate") with alcohol shortly before the performance to cope with anxiety.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-10) Later that evening he was seen at the Nostromo restaurant together with Dalida, other friends and colleagues. He left early, leaving the group behind.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

At approximately 2 in the morning of 27 January, Tenco was found dead in his room, No. 219, at the Hotel Savoy by Dalida.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-12) Tenco died from a single gunshot wound to the head. His death was ultimately ruled a suicide.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-:1-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-nytimes-14) However, due to multiple violations in the investigation, the case was reopened twice, still with a verdict of a suicide.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-tg24-1)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Tenco was apparently upset after learning that his song had been eliminated from the final competition.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-nytimes-14) Several people close to Tenco witnessed that he was more upset with the corruption and bribery at the festival and planned to hold a press conference to unveil it all.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-corriere2021-8)

Tenco was buried in Ricaldone in a small ceremony, while the festival officials kept the show going and tried to evade a scandal. Almost no colleagues were present at the funeral.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-15)

### The inquiry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: The inquiry")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/87/Tomba_Luigi_Tenco.jpg/250px-Tomba_Luigi_Tenco.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tomba_Luigi_Tenco.jpg)

Grave of Luigi Tenco

Initially ruled as a suicide, Tenco's case was reopened in 2005–2009 and then again in 2013–2015.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-17)

In 2004, on TV program _[Domenica in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domenica\_in "Domenica in")_, commissario Arrigo Molinari, the detective who led the case, when asked by host [Paolo Bonolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Bonolis "Paolo Bonolis"), stated that he was sure that Tenco did not commit suicide and defined his death as "a collective murder".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-18) He also justified his own faults concerning the Tenco inquiry by declaring that he had been prevented from investigating properly. In 1967, upon learning of Tenco's death from Dalida and still in his own home, Molinari phoned ANSA and declared that the singer had killed himself. All this took place before he had arrived at the Savoy and before the forensic team could intervene. Shortly after the quoted 2004 interview, Molinari was stabbed to death in his own hotel in [Andora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andora "Andora").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

In 1967, no [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") was performed on the singer's corpse, and no paraffin test or calligraphic analysis on the [suicide note](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_note "Suicide note") with which he explained his final gesture were done.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-19) Some police photographs from the scene, unedited and publicly shown only in 1994, showed that Tenco's body and face was bruised. On the back side of his head a trauma was evident, which forensics didn't confirm to be related to post-mortem falling. Additionally, the concierge of the Savoy, when asked if he had seen Tenco return that night, stated that the keys were not on the reception desk and not that he had seen Tenco return. Traces of sand were spotted on Tenco's hair, clothes and in his car, though journalists confirmed that the car was washed before going to Nostromo.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Dalida testified that on the night of 26 January, while still at the Nostromo, she received a phone call from the Hotel Londra in Sanremo. She told diners she had been notified that Tenco was at the Savoy and was feeling unwell. Dalida did not rush to the Savoy, which was about five minutes away, instead stopping to buy cigarettes and then picking up her ex-husband, Lucien Morisse. They arrived at the Savoy after 40 minutes, where she discovered Tenco's lifeless body.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Notably, the alleged farewell note does not appear in the police report, as it was not found in room 219 on the night of Tenco's death. In fact, the note came into the hands of the police from a third party. Initially, in Dalida's room, No. 104, she gave it to Tenco's friend Sergio Modugno, who passed it on to Piero Vivarelli, a journalist and another of Tenco's friends, who finally gave it to the police. The note read: "I cared for the Italian public and I dedicated in vain five years of my life to them. I'm doing this not because I'm tired of life (I'm not) but as a gesture of dissent against the public who chose 'Io, tu e le rose' for the final night and against the commission that selected 'La rivoluzione'. I hope this will clear somebody's head." Forensics later detected word casts on the note, as if there had been at least one other sheet with different writing superimposed on the one found. The words in the casts are ‘gioco’ (game) and ‘già’ (already). Game, in particular, would seem compatible with Tenco's intention to denounce clandestine betting, as he had announced to his fiancée Valeria in the above-mentioned telephone call. One of the police photos of commissario Molinari showed him standing at the scene with two sheets of paper. Moreover, experts never confirmed the signature on the note to be Tenco's and noted a spelling mistake that a native speaker of Italian who dealt with writing daily would not have made. The family also didn't recognize the handwriting as Tenco's. As supposed by journalists, the alleged suicide note may have been the last page of a document written by Tenco for a different aim.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-20)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

The Italian judicial system later began re-examining Luigi Tenco's suicide. It was pointed out that the bullet hole was on the left temple, while the singer was right-handed. On 15 February 2006, Italian police exhumed Tenco's body for further investigation.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-exhumation-21) The next day, results from the new [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") and [ballistics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistics "Ballistics") analysis were reported. According to Italian experts, what had been thought to be the entry hole on Tenco's left temple was actually the exit site. The bullet [trajectory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajectory "Trajectory") was said to be compatible with suicide.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-:1-13)

Nevertheless, criminologists Pasquale Ragone and Nicola Guarneri, in their book _Le ombre del silenzio_ (_The shadows of silence_, 2013), pointed out several incongruences between the shell casing of the bullet found in Tenco's room and the bullet Tenco's [Walther PPK](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_PPK "Walther PPK") handgun would fire. Professor of ballistic forensics Martino Farneti proved that they did not match. As there was no proof or official statement declaring that Tenco's Walther PPK was actually present in his room the night he died, and police registers show that the pistol was actually found in his car, Guarneri and Ragone wrote that Tenco may have been killed. The actual weapon may have been a [Beretta 70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beretta_70 "Beretta 70"), as it is possible to put a silencer on this type of handgun (similar to a Walther PPK). In fact, no one heard the sound of gunshots the night Tenco died, not even singer [Lucio Dalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucio_Dalla "Lucio Dalla"), whose room was next to Tenco's, or journalist Sandro Ciotti, whose room was opposite Tenco's.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6) At the time of Tenco's death, a door to the inner garden was located only three meters from room 2019, the same one used by police to transport the body.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

In 1993, journalists Marco Buttazzi and Andrea Pomati rediscovered the file compiled by the police in 1967. In the attached photos, they saw that Tenco's legs (from ankles to feet) were positioned under a wooden cabinet. Suspicious of the anomalous position of the corpse, they investigated further and found out that the photos did not depict the real crime scene. They interviewed the undertaker from the case, who stated that commissario Molinari had ordered the body to be immediately transferred to the morgue and before the arrival of the forensic team; it was then taken back to the Savoy and reassembled to allow the photos to be taken and attached to the above-mentioned file.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

Music producer and friend [Paolo Dossena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Dossena "Paolo Dossena") stated that he drove Tenco's car from Rome, where the songwriter lived, to Sanremo. On the way, while passing through a roadblock on the [Aurelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Aurelia "Via Aurelia"), he discovered that Tenco had his Walther PPK in the dashboard of his car. He later confronted the songwriter, who confessed that he had a gun because someone in the past few weeks had tried to force him off a steep road near [Santa Margherita Ligure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Margherita_Ligure "Santa Margherita Ligure") while he was driving.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolteni2015-23)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

In the early '90s, Tenco's older brother Valentino met a woman, Valeria, who had in her possession several letters written by Tenco himself that stated that they had been engaged, their relationship starting in 1964 and lasting until his death. In one of these letters, Tenco writes that his relationship with Dalida was nothing but a clumsy attempt to forget Valeria, who, months before, had left him. He describes Dalida as: "spoiled, neurotic, ignorant, who rejects the idea of being defeated in her profession as in private life". Valentino Tenco identified those letters as written by his brother.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

To date, besides the official conclusion of suicide, journalists have come up with three theories:

*   A robbery gone bad — on 26 January, Tenco won almost 3 million liras at a casino, but the money was never found after his death;
*   A murder of jealousy — Morisse, Dalida's ex-husband, was seen leaving room 219. Morisse was known as an incredibly jealous man who tried to control Dalida and her affairs even after their divorce;
*   A murder to prevent Tenco from causing a scandal by uncovering the bribery and corruption schemes at the Sanremo Festival.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-bergamonews-11)

## Tributes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Luigi_Tenco&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Tributes")]

Shortly after Tenco's death, his friend and songwriter Fabrizio De André wrote the song _Preghiera in gennaio_ (A prayer in January) for him, in which he describes a benevolent God welcoming those who committed suicide into Heaven despite the moral condemnation of the bigots.

In 1974, the [Tenco Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Club_Tenco "Club Tenco") was established, and has been held every year since in Sanremo. Many of the most renowned Italian singer-songwriters from the 1970s explicitly declared Tenco's influence on their work. [Francesco De Gregori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_De_Gregori "Francesco De Gregori")'s album _[Bufalo Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bufalo\_Bill "Bufalo Bill")_ of 1976 contained a song, "Festival", about Tenco's suicide; it points out the hypocrisy with which the music establishment tried to minimize the dramatic event, to let the show go on.

In 1999, the play _Solitudini – Luigi Tenco e [Dalida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalida "Dalida")_, written and directed by Maurizio Valtieri, was performed in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").

French journalist and novelist Philippe Brunel wrote a fiction book, _La nuit de San Remo_ ("The night of Sanremo"), in which he dramatises the arduous search for the truth about Tenco's death.

In 2005, the French television channel [TV5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV5MONDE "TV5MONDE") carried a full-length dramatisation of the love affair between Tenco and Dalida. Tenco was played by [Alessandro Gassman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alessandro_Gassman "Alessandro Gassman"), and Dalida by [Sabrina Ferilli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabrina_Ferilli "Sabrina Ferilli").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Tenco#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuarneriRagone2013-6)

Musical artist

**Umberto Bindi** (12 May 1932 – 23 May 2002) was an Italian singer-songwriter. He is especially known for the popular song he co-wrote with [Gino Paoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Paoli "Gino Paoli"), _Il Mio Mondo_ ("[You're My World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You're_My_World "You're My World")"), which he recorded in Italian in 1963, and ''La musica è finita'' ("[Our Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Song_(Jack_Jones_song) "Our Song (Jack Jones song)")", recorded by [Robert Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Plant "Robert Plant") on 45 rpm and then on album _[Sixty Six to Timbuktu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixty\_Six\_to\_Timbuktu "Sixty Six to Timbuktu")_). It was later performed by singers in English and other languages.

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Umberto_Bindi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

Bindi was born in [Bogliasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogliasco "Bogliasco") ([Province of Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Genoa "Province of Genoa")), Italy, and was classically trained. He wrote his first song, "T'ho perduto" ("I've Lost You"), in 1950. He made his professional debut in Italian popular music in 1959 with his composition, "[Arrivederci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrivederci_(song) "Arrivederci (song)")". The song was recorded by [Don Marino Barreto Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Marino_Barreto_Jr. "Don Marino Barreto Jr."), and soon became the best-selling single in Italy for that year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-1) A [cover version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") was recorded by [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker") in 1960 for the Italian film, _Urlatori alla sbarra_.

Bindi's first album, _Umberto Bindi e le sue canzoni_, was released in 1960. Bindi also wrote and recorded a number of songs that would make him known to the larger public in Italy. A few of these became classic hits there, covered many times: besides "Arrivederci", _[Il Nostro Concerto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Nostro\_Concerto "Il Nostro Concerto")_ ("Our Concert"), 1960, number 2 on Italy's best-selling singles list for the year,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-2) "Riviera" (1961), and "Il Mio Mondo". The latter was recorded in English in 1964 by the British pop singer [Cilla Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cilla_Black "Cilla Black"), and remained number 1 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") for four weeks, while also reaching Number 1 in Australia, Number 2 in Ireland and New Zealand and Number 26 in the USA.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-3) Bindi's "Il Nostro Concerto" spent one week in the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") in November 1960, at number 47.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums_2-4)

He also wrote the music of _La musica è finita_ (1967), another Italian classic, made famous by [Ornella Vanoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornella_Vanoni "Ornella Vanoni") and [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina_(Italian_singer) "Mina (Italian singer)").

However, his singing career in Italy stalled, and he and music critics attributed this to the Italian media's discomfort in the 1960s with Bindi's homosexuality.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-5) The singer nevertheless made a few concert appearances.

Bindi died at a [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") hospital from [heart disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_disease "Cardiovascular disease") at the age of 70.

Musical artist

**Umberto Bindi** (12 May 1932 – 23 May 2002) was an Italian singer-songwriter. He is especially known for the popular song he co-wrote with [Gino Paoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Paoli "Gino Paoli"), _Il Mio Mondo_ ("[You're My World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You're_My_World "You're My World")"), which he recorded in Italian in 1963, and ''La musica è finita'' ("[Our Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Our_Song_(Jack_Jones_song) "Our Song (Jack Jones song)")", recorded by [Robert Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Plant "Robert Plant") on 45 rpm and then on album _[Sixty Six to Timbuktu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixty\_Six\_to\_Timbuktu "Sixty Six to Timbuktu")_). It was later performed by singers in English and other languages.

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Umberto_Bindi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

Bindi was born in [Bogliasco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bogliasco "Bogliasco") ([Province of Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province_of_Genoa "Province of Genoa")), Italy, and was classically trained. He wrote his first song, "T'ho perduto" ("I've Lost You"), in 1950. He made his professional debut in Italian popular music in 1959 with his composition, "[Arrivederci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrivederci_(song) "Arrivederci (song)")". The song was recorded by [Don Marino Barreto Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Marino_Barreto_Jr. "Don Marino Barreto Jr."), and soon became the best-selling single in Italy for that year.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-1) A [cover version](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cover_version "Cover version") was recorded by [Chet Baker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chet_Baker "Chet Baker") in 1960 for the Italian film, _Urlatori alla sbarra_.

Bindi's first album, _Umberto Bindi e le sue canzoni_, was released in 1960. Bindi also wrote and recorded a number of songs that would make him known to the larger public in Italy. A few of these became classic hits there, covered many times: besides "Arrivederci", _[Il Nostro Concerto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_Nostro\_Concerto "Il Nostro Concerto")_ ("Our Concert"), 1960, number 2 on Italy's best-selling singles list for the year,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-2) "Riviera" (1961), and "Il Mio Mondo". The latter was recorded in English in 1964 by the British pop singer [Cilla Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cilla_Black "Cilla Black"), and remained number 1 on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") for four weeks, while also reaching Number 1 in Australia, Number 2 in Ireland and New Zealand and Number 26 in the USA.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-3) Bindi's "Il Nostro Concerto" spent one week in the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart") in November 1960, at number 47.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums_2-4)

He also wrote the music of _La musica è finita_ (1967), another Italian classic, made famous by [Ornella Vanoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornella_Vanoni "Ornella Vanoni") and [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina_(Italian_singer) "Mina (Italian singer)").

However, his singing career in Italy stalled, and he and music critics attributed this to the Italian media's discomfort in the 1960s with Bindi's homosexuality.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Bindi#cite_note-5) The singer nevertheless made a few concert appearances.

Bindi died at a [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome") hospital from [heart disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiovascular_disease "Cardiovascular disease") at the age of 70.

**Adriano Celentano** (Italian:[[adriˈaːno tʃelenˈtaːno]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); born 6 January 1938) is an Italian singer-songwriter, actor, showman, and filmmaker. He is dubbed _Il Molleggiato_ ('the springy one') because of his energetic dancing.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-3)

Celentano's many albums frequently enjoyed both commercial and critical success. With around 150 million records sold worldwide, he is one of [the best-selling Italian musical artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_estimated_best-selling_Italian_music_artists "List of estimated best-selling Italian music artists").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-5) Often credited as the author of both the music and lyrics of his songs, according to his wife [Claudia Mori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudia_Mori "Claudia Mori"), some were written in collaboration with others. Due to his prolific career, both in Italy and abroad, he is considered one of the pillars of [Italian music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Italy "Music of Italy").

Celentano is recognized for being particularly perceptive of changes in the music business and is credited for having introduced rock and roll to Italy. As an actor, Celentano has appeared in 39 films, mostly comedies.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adriano_Celentano&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Celentano was born on 6 January 1938 in [Greco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco_(district_of_Milan) "Greco (district of Milan)"), [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"), Italy, at 14 Via Cristoforo Gluck, a street close to the Central Station and this address later became the subject of the famous song "[Il ragazzo della via Gluck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_ragazzo_della_via_Gluck "Il ragazzo della via Gluck")" ('The boy from Gluck Street'). His parents, Leontino Celentano and Giuditta Giuva, were from [Foggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foggia "Foggia"), Apulia, and had moved north for work.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-6) His career as a singer started in 1959. Before his debut as an artist, he was working as a [watchmaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchmaker "Watchmaker").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-7)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adriano_Celentano&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Piginicelentano.jpg/250px-Piginicelentano.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Piginicelentano.jpg)

Celentano with an [Eko Guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eko_Guitars "Eko Guitars")

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Mina_Celentano_1967.jpg/250px-Mina_Celentano_1967.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mina_Celentano_1967.jpg)

Celentano with [Mina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mina_(Italian_singer) "Mina (Italian singer)") in 1967

Heavily influenced by [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") and the 1950s rock 'n' roll scene as well as by American actor [Jerry Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Lewis "Jerry Lewis"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-8) Celentano started playing in a rock and roll band with [Giorgio Gaber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gaber "Giorgio Gaber") and [Enzo Jannacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Jannacci "Enzo Jannacci"). Along with Gaber and Jannacci, he was discovered by Jolly Records A&R Executive [Ezio Leoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezio_Leoni "Ezio Leoni"), who signed him to his first recording contract and co-authored with Celentano some of his greatest early hits, including "[24.000 baci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24.000_baci "24.000 baci")", "Il tuo bacio è come un rock", and "Si è spento il Sole". He first appeared on screen in _[Ragazzi del Juke-Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragazzi\_del\_Juke-Box "Ragazzi del Juke-Box")_, a 1959 Italian musical film directed by [Lucio Fulci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucio_Fulci "Lucio Fulci") with music by Ezio Leoni. In 1960, [Federico Fellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Fellini "Federico Fellini") cast him as a rock and roll singer in his film _[La dolce vita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_dolce\_vita "La dolce vita")_ (1960).

In 1962, Celentano founded the Italian record label [Clan Celentano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Celentano "Clan Celentano") (which is still active) with many performers such as [Don Backy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Backy "Don Backy"), [Ola & the Janglers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ola_&_the_Janglers "Ola & the Janglers"), [Ricky Gianco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Gianco "Ricky Gianco"), [Katty Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katty_Line?action=edit&redlink=1 "Katty Line (page does not exist)"), [Gino Santercole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Santercole "Gino Santercole"), [Fred Bongusto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bongusto "Fred Bongusto") and his wife [Claudia Mori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudia_Mori "Claudia Mori").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

As a film director, Celentano frequently cast [Ornella Muti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornella_Muti "Ornella Muti"), [Eleonora Giorgi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleonora_Giorgi "Eleonora Giorgi") and his wife Claudia Mori. He and Mori have three children, Rosita, Giacomo and [Rosalinda Celentano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalinda_Celentano "Rosalinda Celentano"). Rosalinda is most notable to worldwide audiences for playing [Satan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan "Satan") in [Mel Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Gibson "Mel Gibson")'s _[The Passion of the Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Passion\_of\_the\_Christ "The Passion of the Christ")_. Celentano has also hosted several Italian television shows.

Celentano has retained his popularity in Italy for over 50 years, selling millions of records and appearing in numerous TV shows and movies. As part of his TV and movie work, he created a comic genre, with a characteristic walk and facial expressions. For the most part, his films were commercially successful; indeed, in the 1970s and part of the 1980s, his low-budget movies were top of Italian box office rankings. As an actor, critics point to _[Serafino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serafino\_(film) "Serafino (film)")_ (1968), directed by [Pietro Germi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Germi "Pietro Germi"), as his best performance.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/40/%D0%A7%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8.jpg/250px-%D0%A7%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%A7%D0%B5%D0%BB%D0%B5%D0%BD%D1%82%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%BE_%D0%9C%D0%BE%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B8.jpg)

Celentano (right) in 2012 with [Gianni Morandi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Morandi "Gianni Morandi")

He has released 40 albums, consisting of 29 studio albums, three live albums, and eight compilations. Among his most popular songs there are "La coppia più bella del mondo", which sold over one million copies, and was awarded a [gold disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification");[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-The_Book_of_Golden_Discs-9) "[Azzurro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azzurro "Azzurro")" (1968), written by [Paolo Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Conte "Paolo Conte"), "[Svalutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalutation "Svalutation")" (1976), and "[Prisencolinensinainciusol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisencolinensinainciusol "Prisencolinensinainciusol")" (1972), which was written to mimic the way English sounds to non-English speakers despite being almost entirely gibberish.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-:0-10)

Celentano was referenced in the 1979 [Ian Dury and the Blockheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blockheads "The Blockheads") song and single, "[Reasons to Be Cheerful, Part 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reasons_to_Be_Cheerful,_Part_3 "Reasons to Be Cheerful, Part 3")", as one of the aforementioned "reasons to be cheerful", and in [Fellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Fellini "Federico Fellini")'s 1986 film _[Ginger and Fred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginger\_and\_Fred "Ginger and Fred")_.

After 18 years without live performances, Celentano's 2012 live concert was broadcast on [Mediaset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediaset "Mediaset") channel [Canale 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canale_5 "Canale 5"), attracting over 9 million viewers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-11)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adriano_Celentano&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Celentano has been a [vegetarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetarianism "Vegetarianism") since 2005 and has defended [animal rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_rights "Animal rights").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-13) A football fan, Celentano is a well-known [Inter Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_Milan "Inter Milan") supporter.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-14) In 2009, Celentano told _[La Repubblica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Repubblica "La Repubblica")_ that for years he wanted to learn English but never found time to do so, and said it is a "real pain" not being able to speak the language.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-15)

When the [Barilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barilla_(company) "Barilla (company)") pasta company introduced a corkscrew pasta in the 1970s, it was named _cellentani_ for Celentano. As Barilla trademarked the name, other companies call the shape _cavatappi_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-16)

**Adriano Celentano** (Italian:[[adriˈaːno tʃelenˈtaːno]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Italian "Help:IPA/Italian"); born 6 January 1938) is an Italian singer-songwriter, actor, showman, and filmmaker. He is dubbed _Il Molleggiato_ ('the springy one') because of his energetic dancing.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-3)

Celentano's many albums frequently enjoyed both commercial and critical success. With around 150 million records sold worldwide, he is one of [the best-selling Italian musical artists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_estimated_best-selling_Italian_music_artists "List of estimated best-selling Italian music artists").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-5) Often credited as the author of both the music and lyrics of his songs, according to his wife [Claudia Mori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudia_Mori "Claudia Mori"), some were written in collaboration with others. Due to his prolific career, both in Italy and abroad, he is considered one of the pillars of [Italian music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_of_Italy "Music of Italy").

Celentano is recognized for being particularly perceptive of changes in the music business and is credited for having introduced rock and roll to Italy. As an actor, Celentano has appeared in 39 films, mostly comedies.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adriano_Celentano&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Celentano was born on 6 January 1938 in [Greco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco_(district_of_Milan) "Greco (district of Milan)"), [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"), Italy, at 14 Via Cristoforo Gluck, a street close to the Central Station and this address later became the subject of the famous song "[Il ragazzo della via Gluck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il_ragazzo_della_via_Gluck "Il ragazzo della via Gluck")" ('The boy from Gluck Street'). His parents, Leontino Celentano and Giuditta Giuva, were from [Foggia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foggia "Foggia"), Apulia, and had moved north for work.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-6) His career as a singer started in 1959. Before his debut as an artist, he was working as a [watchmaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watchmaker "Watchmaker").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-7)

Heavily influenced by [Elvis Presley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elvis_Presley "Elvis Presley") and the 1950s rock 'n' roll scene as well as by American actor [Jerry Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Lewis "Jerry Lewis"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-8) Celentano started playing in a rock and roll band with [Giorgio Gaber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Gaber "Giorgio Gaber") and [Enzo Jannacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzo_Jannacci "Enzo Jannacci"). Along with Gaber and Jannacci, he was discovered by Jolly Records A&R Executive [Ezio Leoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezio_Leoni "Ezio Leoni"), who signed him to his first recording contract and co-authored with Celentano some of his greatest early hits, including "[24.000 baci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24.000_baci "24.000 baci")", "Il tuo bacio è come un rock", and "Si è spento il Sole". He first appeared on screen in _[Ragazzi del Juke-Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ragazzi\_del\_Juke-Box "Ragazzi del Juke-Box")_, a 1959 Italian musical film directed by [Lucio Fulci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucio_Fulci "Lucio Fulci") with music by Ezio Leoni. In 1960, [Federico Fellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Fellini "Federico Fellini") cast him as a rock and roll singer in his film _[La dolce vita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_dolce\_vita "La dolce vita")_ (1960).

In 1962, Celentano founded the Italian record label [Clan Celentano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clan_Celentano "Clan Celentano") (which is still active) with many performers such as [Don Backy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Backy "Don Backy"), [Ola & the Janglers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ola_&_the_Janglers "Ola & the Janglers"), [Ricky Gianco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricky_Gianco "Ricky Gianco"), [Katty Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katty_Line?action=edit&redlink=1 "Katty Line (page does not exist)"), [Gino Santercole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gino_Santercole "Gino Santercole"), [Fred Bongusto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Bongusto "Fred Bongusto") and his wife [Claudia Mori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudia_Mori "Claudia Mori").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

As a film director, Celentano frequently cast [Ornella Muti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornella_Muti "Ornella Muti"), [Eleonora Giorgi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eleonora_Giorgi "Eleonora Giorgi") and his wife Claudia Mori. He and Mori have three children, Rosita, Giacomo and [Rosalinda Celentano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosalinda_Celentano "Rosalinda Celentano"). Rosalinda is most notable to worldwide audiences for playing [Satan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satan "Satan") in [Mel Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mel_Gibson "Mel Gibson")'s _[The Passion of the Christ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Passion\_of\_the\_Christ "The Passion of the Christ")_. Celentano has also hosted several Italian television shows.

Celentano has retained his popularity in Italy for over 50 years, selling millions of records and appearing in numerous TV shows and movies. As part of his TV and movie work, he created a comic genre, with a characteristic walk and facial expressions. For the most part, his films were commercially successful; indeed, in the 1970s and part of the 1980s, his low-budget movies were top of Italian box office rankings. As an actor, critics point to _[Serafino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serafino\_(film) "Serafino (film)")_ (1968), directed by [Pietro Germi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pietro_Germi "Pietro Germi"), as his best performance.

Celentano (right) in 2012 with [Gianni Morandi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gianni_Morandi "Gianni Morandi")

He has released 40 albums, consisting of 29 studio albums, three live albums, and eight compilations. Among his most popular songs there are "La coppia più bella del mondo", which sold over one million copies, and was awarded a [gold disc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_recording_certification "Music recording certification");[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-The_Book_of_Golden_Discs-9) "[Azzurro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azzurro "Azzurro")" (1968), written by [Paolo Conte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Conte "Paolo Conte"), "[Svalutation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Svalutation "Svalutation")" (1976), and "[Prisencolinensinainciusol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisencolinensinainciusol "Prisencolinensinainciusol")" (1972), which was written to mimic the way English sounds to non-English speakers despite being almost entirely gibberish.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-:0-10)

Celentano was referenced in the 1979 [Ian Dury and the Blockheads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blockheads "The Blockheads") song and single, "[Reasons to Be Cheerful, Part 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reasons_to_Be_Cheerful,_Part_3 "Reasons to Be Cheerful, Part 3")", as one of the aforementioned "reasons to be cheerful", and in [Fellini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Fellini "Federico Fellini")'s 1986 film _[Ginger and Fred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ginger\_and\_Fred "Ginger and Fred")_.

After 18 years without live performances, Celentano's 2012 live concert was broadcast on [Mediaset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediaset "Mediaset") channel [Canale 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canale_5 "Canale 5"), attracting over 9 million viewers.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-11)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adriano_Celentano&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Celentano has been a [vegetarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetarianism "Vegetarianism") since 2005 and has defended [animal rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_rights "Animal rights").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-13) A football fan, Celentano is a well-known [Inter Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter_Milan "Inter Milan") supporter.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-14) In 2009, Celentano told _[La Repubblica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Repubblica "La Repubblica")_ that for years he wanted to learn English but never found time to do so, and said it is a "real pain" not being able to speak the language.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-15)

When the [Barilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barilla_(company) "Barilla (company)") pasta company introduced a corkscrew pasta in the 1970s, it was named _cellentani_ for Celentano. As Barilla trademarked the name, other companies call the shape _cavatappi_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriano_Celentano#cite_note-16)
